name: Wei Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the grill at Hollis Steakhouse, a family-owned place on the high street in a small town, and I've been there four years. I come in at two, light the charcoal grill, portion the steaks and do my mise en place, which just means getting every sauce and garnish ready before service. From six it's tickets non-stop until ten, sometimes eighty covers on a Friday, and I love that rush when the whole line is in step. What wears me out is the burns on my forearms, the heat, and finishing at midnight with my back gone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's around you, at work and at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: At work it's Gordon, the head chef, who's fair but tired, and Lena on the fryer, who's been my lunch-break mate for years. At home it's me and my partner Rosa in a small rented flat above a laundrette, and she does home care visits for the council. Between us we just about cover rent and bills, and at the end of most months there's maybe forty quid left. There aren't many proper kitchens round here either, maybe three that would take a grill cook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so, it was all hype from people selling software. At work I'd probably joke with Lena that the robots aren't coming for our tongs after all. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something about how the money should have gone into nurses and care workers instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it doesn't change my real problem, which is that I'm one broken fridge away from not making rent. Hollis has had two quiet winters, and Gordon already cut my Tuesday shift last January. So AI or no AI, I'm still on lower pay in a town with three kitchens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep doing the grill, because I don't want to rock anything. I'd ask Gordon straight out for my Tuesday back before Christmas, because that's about two hundred a month. And I'd push Rosa's idea of joining the hospitality workers' union, even though it makes me nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels flat, not scary exactly, more like the same grey worry I already carry. The hype going away doesn't put money in my account. I still check my balance before I buy a coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the union makes you nervous. Why is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Mr Hollis is old school and I don't know how he'd take it. I believe in unions, my granddad was a docker and swore by his, but I'm not brave about it. I'd want Lena to join with me so it's not just my name on a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight this winter, what goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My phone contract would go to the cheapest one, that's the first thing. Then we'd stop getting the Friday takeaway, which is funny when I cook all day. After that I honestly don't know, maybe I'd ask my mum, and I hate asking my mum.

say: I'd say the AI hype was **mostly sales talk** from tech firms.
I'd say the money should have gone into **care workers and nurses** instead.
think: I think my real problem is a **thin cushion**, not robots.
I think one cut shift or **broken fridge** could put me behind on rent.
do: Ask Gordon to restore the **Tuesday shift** worth about two hundred a month.
Join the **hospitality union** with Lena, despite feeling nervous about the owner.
feel: He feels a **flat, familiar worry** that the end of the hype doesn't fix.
S0.quote: I'm one broken fridge away from not making rent.
fieldNote: Wei's **money worry** is already there, so the plateau barely moves his mood.
His **pro-union views** clash with his fear of standing out to the owner.
He blames **tech firms** for wasted money, but his real enemy is short hours.

steps.text: Ask the head chef for the lost Tuesday shift back
Join the hospitality workers' union together with Lena
Switch to the cheapest phone plan and stop Friday takeaways

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people's turn to worry for once, not us. At work I'd tell everyone that a robot can't feel when a steak's done by pressing it. Online I'd say any company using AI should pay a tax that goes to the workers it pushes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the bit that changes first is around me, not on my grill. The ordering and the rota would go onto some app, and Gordon's already said the booking system is going to some AI thing. What worries me is the next step, someone selling Mr Hollis a machine that flips burgers, because Hollis does a lot of burgers at lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the grill and not touch any of the apps unless they make me. I'd sign the union petition about robots in kitchens, and I'd go to the meeting in the city if Rosa came with me. And I'd try to put fifty a month aside, even if that means fewer nights out with Lena.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like waiting for a bus that you know is going to hit you, just slowly. I'm uneasy all the time, and the thin money makes it worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't touch the apps unless made to. What if Gordon asks you to use one for ordering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do it, I'm not going to lose my job over a tablet. But I'd be slow and I'd hate it, and I'd probably ask Lena to show me twice. I've never used any of that AI stuff, not even on my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the kitchen would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My workmate Lena is on the fryer, and the fryer is the easiest station to put a machine on. You just drop baskets and shake them, a machine could do that tomorrow. She's got a teenage brother she helps out, so she can't lose hours either.

say: I'd say firms using AI should pay a **robot tax** to the workers they push out.
I'd tell the kitchen that **no machine** can judge a steak by pressing it.
think: I think the **ordering and rota** move to apps first, then machines come for the lunch burgers.
I think a **burger-flipping machine** at lunch would cut my hours before my job.
do: Sign the **union petition** on kitchen robots and attend the city meeting with Rosa.
Save **fifty a month** by cutting nights out with Lena.
Use the **ordering tablet** only if the head chef insists.
feel: He feels **slow-motion dread**, made worse by having almost no savings.
S1.quote: My workmate Lena is on the fryer, and the fryer is the easiest station to put a machine on.
fieldNote: Wei sees **hands-on work** as safer, yet worries about cheap lunch-time automation.
He'd accept **new tech** only under orders, and leans on Lena to learn it.
He thinks first about **Lena's hours**, which shows his solidarity is personal.

steps.text: Sign the union petition against robots in restaurant kitchens
Put fifty a month aside by skipping nights out
Keep working the charcoal grill and avoid the apps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in, and fast. At work I'd say they should make it law that restaurants keep a human on every station. Online I'd share every petition going, honestly, and I'd be angry in the comments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think with two years of warning I'm behind before I even start. The thinking stuff goes in 2028, so Gordon's ordering and the bookings vanish, but I'd still have the grill until around 2031. That's maybe five years of work left, and I've got nothing saved and no other trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing I'd do is join the union properly and go to every meeting. I'd ask about any free course the council runs, maybe care work like Rosa, because people will still want a human holding their hand. And I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent, food or the bus pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the floor going soft under me. I lie awake doing sums in my head, and the sums don't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the grill stays until about 2031. What does that three-year gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm not first out the door, but I'm not safe either. Three years sounds long until you remember I couldn't even save for a holiday in the last three. I'd use it to try care work part time, to see if I can stand it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Rosa the night you first heard this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we need to stop pretending it'll sort itself out. She'd probably say her job's safer than mine, and she'd be right, which is a strange thing to feel. I'd tell my partner Rosa that I might need to lean on her wage for a while, and that would sting.

say: I'd say the government must **make it law** to keep a human on every station.
I'd share **every petition** going and argue in the comments online.
think: I think I've got about **five years** of grill work left before robots arrive.
I think having **no savings** means I start behind with only two years' warning.
do: Join the **union** fully and attend every branch meeting.
Try a free **council care course** and do some care shifts part time.
Cut spending to **rent, food** and the bus pass only.
feel: He feels like the **floor is going soft**, lying awake doing sums that don't add up.
S2.quote: I'd tell my partner Rosa that I might need to lean on her wage for a while, and that would sting.
fieldNote: Wei sees the **three-year robot gap** as a delay, not as safety.
He turns to **care work** because it's what Rosa knows and feels human.
His **resistance to tech** leaves him no route into kitchen machines or AI roles.

steps.text: Go to every hospitality union branch meeting
Sign up for the council's free care work course
Cut spending to rent, food and the bus pass
Lean on Rosa's care wage while switching jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say it's on the government and the big tech companies to sort out. At work I'd be the one pushing for a meeting about what Mr Hollis plans to do with the kitchen. Online I'd say five years is plenty of time to plan, so there's no excuse for leaving workers in the dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with five years I could actually do something, but I'm scared I'd waste it. Thinking AI by 2031 means the head chef's paperwork goes, but robots wouldn't hit the grill line until around 2034. That's eight years of grill work, which is more than I've done so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the care course part time next year while I still have the grill shifts. I'd try to build up one month of rent in savings, which would be a first for me. And I'd vote for whoever promises to tax the robot companies and fund retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels heavy but not hopeless. More like a long, worried countdown than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you hate new tech. Would you consider working with the kitchen robots instead of leaving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if someone trained me properly and paid me for the training. But I know myself, I'm the last person to learn a new till. I'd rather go somewhere a human is the point of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would getting one month's rent saved actually take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About six hundred, so fifty a month for a year, which sounds easy and isn't. I'd have to stop buying lunch on shift and eat staff meal only. Rosa would do the same, and we'd keep the jar on the kitchen shelf so we see it.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough warning that leaving workers in the dark is inexcusable.
I'd push for a **kitchen meeting** about the owner's plans.
think: I think I have about **eight years** of grill work before robots reach the line.
I think I'm likely to **waste the time** unless I start something soon.
do: Start a **care course** part time next year alongside grill shifts.
Save **one month's rent**, about six hundred, over a year.
Vote for parties that **tax robot firms** and fund retraining.
feel: He feels a **long, worried countdown** rather than a sudden cliff.
S3.quote: Thinking AI by 2031 means the head chef's paperwork goes, but robots wouldn't hit the grill line until around 2034.
fieldNote: More time gives Wei a **concrete plan**, but he expects to lose the job eventually.
He would rather **leave cooking** than learn to run kitchen machines.
His savings goal of **six hundred** shows how thin his cushion really is.

steps.text: Start a part-time care course next year
Save six hundred in a jar for one month's rent
Vote for parties promising robot taxes and retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so the government has no excuses. At work I'd say let's get the union in now, while things are calm. Online I'd probably say less, because a decade away feels like forever to most people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I could cook until I'm about forty, since the robots wouldn't hit kitchens until around 2039. That's a lot of my working life, but it's not all of it. The thing that still bothers me is that I'd hit forty with no new trade if I just sat there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the grill and get the union into Hollis over the next couple of years. I'd do the care course slowly, maybe one module a year, so I have something by my mid-thirties. And Rosa and I would try to save for a deposit, though honestly that might not happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels less scary, a bit like a long road with a sign at the end. I'd still worry, because I always worry, but I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you always worry. Is that about AI or something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly money, if I'm honest with myself. Even in the hype one, where nothing changes, I'm worried about rent and shifts. Ten years for AI doesn't fix the fact that I earn less than I should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing at forty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to still be cooking, but somewhere I'm paid properly, maybe a hospital or a school kitchen. Places like that feel safer, slower to change. Or doing care work with Rosa, which I never pictured but I could see it.

say: I'd say a **decade** gives government no excuse not to prepare workers.
I'd say get the **union** into the kitchen now while it's calm.
think: I think I can cook until about **forty** before robots reach kitchens.
I think I'd reach forty with **no new trade** if I did nothing.
do: Bring the **union** into Hollis Steakhouse over the next two years.
Take one **care module** a year to have a fallback by thirty-five.
Look for steadier cooking in a **hospital or school** kitchen.
feel: He feels a **steadier worry**, enough to sleep, but money still nags him.
S4.quote: Ten years for AI doesn't fix the fact that I earn less than I should.
fieldNote: With a decade, Wei's fear shifts back to **low pay** rather than AI.
He sees **public kitchens** like hospitals and schools as safer from fast change.
He keeps **care work** as a slow fallback instead of a forced exit.

steps.text: Organise a union branch at Hollis Steakhouse with Lena
Take one care work module each year
Apply for cook jobs in hospital or school kitchens

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time and no money to change anything. What would help is a proper wage while I retrain, not a loan, and some rule that keeps people in kitchens. And the union, honestly, I should have joined years ago.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how much we get paid, and that's the thing under everything. Every question about AI turned into a question about rent. If I earned a bit more, I could face all of this with a bit more courage.

headlineQuote: Every question about AI turned into a question about rent.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old grill cook** at a family steakhouse in a small town.
He lives with his partner Rosa, a **care worker**, and has almost no savings.
He backs **unions and regulation**, but fears standing out to his boss.
He avoids **new technology** and would leave cooking rather than run kitchen robots.
His mood follows **money** more than AI, so even AI Plateau leaves him anxious.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** most, with no time or money to change course.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **paid wage while retraining** and rules keeping humans in kitchens.
He says joining the **union** would help, and wishes he'd done it sooner.
